## Product Overview

The Blackwing 602 Short Pencils are compact, high-quality writing tools designed for those on the go. Perfect for sketching, note-taking, and even tallying golf scores, these pencils fit easily in your pocket or bag.

## Key Benefits

- Compact Size – Half the size of regular Blackwing pencils, perfect for travel.
- Firm Graphite Core – Provides a smooth writing experience.
- Unique Ferrule Design – Features a square ferrule with a pink eraser.
- Stylish Storage Box – Comes in a Blackwing storage box for easy transport.
- Set of 12 – Includes 12 mini pencils in each set.

## Who This Product Is Best For

The Blackwing 602 Short Pencils are ideal for artists, students, and professionals who need a portable writing solution. They're also great for golfers and anyone who enjoys sketching or taking notes on the go.

## Common Questions About This Product

### What is the length of each Blackwing 602 Short pencil?

Each pencil measures 4 3/10 inches in length.

### Are these pencils refillable or do they need to be replaced?

The Blackwing 602 Short pencils are not refillable; they need to be replaced once used up.

### What type of graphite is used in the Blackwing 602 Short pencils?

These pencils feature a firm graphite core, providing a high-quality writing experience.

## Buying Considerations

When choosing the Blackwing 602 Short Pencils, consider their compact size and intended use. They're perfect for travel and sketching, making them a great choice for artists and students alike.

## Product description

# Tools Coveted By Award-winning Creators 

 Pencils, sharpeners and notebooks for writers, artists, composers and anyone who does their best thinking with a pencil in hand. Genuine California Incense-cedar. Japanese graphite. The iconic ferrule that has been our signature for ninety years. 

# Built on Heritage 

 Blackwing's roots go back to the 1930s, when it was the pencil of choice for creators including John Steinbeck and Chuck Jones. The brand disappeared in the 1990s and returned in 2010. Today Blackwing crafts pencils, notebooks and analog tools for people who want to slow down. 

- I'm new to Blackwing. Which pencil should I start with? 

 Most people start with the Pearl - it sits between the soft Matte and the firm 602. To try all four cores before committing to a dozen, the Pencil Essentials Set includes one of each. 
- What do soft, firm, balanced and extra-firm actually mean? 

 They describe how much graphite the pencil lays down and how long it holds a point. Softer cores make darker lines and need sharpening more often. Firmer cores make finer lines and last longer between sharpenings. 
- Will Blackwing pencils fit a standard sharpener? 

 Yes. The barrel is a standard pencil diameter. The Blackwing One-Step and Two-Step sharpeners are shaped to produce the long, curved point these pencils are designed around. 
- Why is the eraser rectangular instead of round? 

 The flat eraser slides out of the ferrule so you can extend it as it wears, then replace it when it is gone. It has been Blackwing's signature since the 1930s. 
- What is the Blackwing Foundation? 

 A portion of every purchase funds the Blackwing Foundation, which supports arts and music education in public schools.

results.title: Palomino Blackwing 602 Pencil Review - the paper kind
results.author: Em
results.text:
Palomino Blackwing 602 Pencil Review - the paper kind

# Palomino Blackwing 602 Pencil Review

 March 7, 2020 / No Comments

I have been wanting to try the Palomino Blackwing 602 Pencil for a long time. I’ve heard so many people talk about how they are great pencils to use for art. Obviously, as a person who does art, I wanted to see what made them so special.

There was only one problem. I’ve said in the past I am not particularly fussy when it comes to writing tools. It if works I’ll use it. There is one exception to this, I hate using regular pencils. I hate that you have to sharpen them, I hate that the lead wears down, and in many cases breaks meaning you have to sharpen them again. I would rather not have to go through all that hassle. So, for the most part, I use mechanical pencils where possible. 

There is also the fact that the Palomino Blackwing pencils are very expensive. Costing around £30 for a box of 12. If you’re in the UK this can go up to £60 depending on stock levels. Despite all this, I decided I would try the Blackwing pencils. To see if they are as good as the rumours I’ve heard. And try to figure out if they are worth that £30 price tag. 

### About The Blackwing 602 Pencil

The original Blackwing pencils date back to the 30s. These pencils were manufactured by the Eberhart Faber Pencil Company. They were the favoured pencil of artists and writers of the time. The Blackwing pencil was used regularly by animators working on the early Disney movies. There is even an exhibition of Walt Disney’s desk in the One Man’s Dream gallery which features Blackwing pencils. Today they are still a favoured tool of many artists. 

The original Blackwing pencils were discontinued in the 90s. According to Wikipedia, this was caused by a breakdown of the machine which made the metal clip that sits inside the ferrule. Vintage Blackwing pencils can still be found on eBay. A single pencil can be found for $40 and some rarer pencils go up to $100. Fortunately, the modern version of the Blackwing 602 can be bought at a slightly more reasonable price. 

In 2010 a Californian based pencil manufacturer bought the Blackwing trademark and began making the pencils again under its Palomino division. In all respects, these new pencils are exactly the same as the ones which have been manufactured since the 30s. 

### The Pencil

There are a number of different types of Palomino Blackwing pencil. But for the purposes of this review, I will be talking about the original Blackwing 602 pencil. These pencils have a hexagonal body with a graphite core encased in Cedarwood. 

The pencils feel really nice to hold, which is an important factor for a pencil. The Blackwing has a gold ferrule on the end of the pencil, containing a small eraser. This ferrule makes the pencil significantly longer than a standard pencil. Combined with the weight of the ferrule the Blackwing pencil may feel slightly off-balance compared to a regular pencil when you start using it. 

This may sound like a small detail but was something I certainly noticed when I first started using my Blackwing 602. Fortunately, this was something I got used to fairly quickly.

The length of the pencil is more of an annoyance. I said that the ferrule adds a bit onto the length. But I think the body of the pencil is also slightly longer than a regular pencil. This caused some problems when I wanted to carry the Blackwing pencil around with me because it doesn’t fit into my pencil case. 

Now admittedly this became less of a problem as I used the pencil. But it was worrying that I had to leave the Blackwing pencil in my rucksack with no other protection. It’s not something I would bother about normally. And it absolutely wasn’t the only writing tool in my rucksack. But while I don’t care that I have a mechanical pencil in some random pocket of my bag. I absolutely cared about the Blackwing because of its price. 

Basically what I’m trying to say is that it was very inconvenient that this pencil did not fit in my pencil case. And I refuse to go out and buy an entire new pencil case just so one specific pencil will fit in it. 

### The Ferrule

I’ve hated using pencils for almost as long as I’ve had to use pencils. I started using mechanical pencils in school as soon as I learned that they were a thing. I loathed using pencils with an eraser on the end, I didn’t see the point of having an eraser on the end of my pencil when it would run out so quickly. 

I’m very happy to say that the Blackwing pencil fixes all the problems I’ve ever had with erasers on pencils. The eraser is held in the metal ferrule, in this is another clip which holds the eraser. Its really easy to pull this clip, and therefore the eraser out of the ferrule. This way you can get the full use of the eraser and replace them when used up. 

I love that this is such a simple solution to something I’ve hated for so long. The metal ferrule also adds to the whole aesthetic of the pencil. I’m not sure if you’d say it makes the pencil look expensive, but it is a nicely designed pencil. 

### Pencil Lead

The Blackwing Pencils come in a number of different graphite hardnesses. The original Blackwing 602 pencil has the hardest graphite out of the three in the Palomino range. According to the Blackwing website, this has been designed to maximise point retention while sacrificing as little darkness as possible. 

The Blackwing 602 Pencil is comparable to a 2B lead. If that means anything to you. Honestly, I’ve been at art school for 2 years now and I still don’t understand the difference between 2B and HB. 

There are another few pencils in the Palomino range which have softer leads if that is something you prefer for drawing. The Blackwing Pearl is slightly softer than the Blackwing 602. The regular Palomino Blackwing is the softest in the range, equivalent to a 4B pencil. 

If you’re buying these pencils for artistic purposed then the hardness of the graphite will be really important. If might be an idea to do some research and figure out which pencil will work best for you. 

The Blackwing 602 pencil I bought has very hard graphite which makes it ideal for writing. I also used this for creating art, but because of the type of illustrations I was doing, a hard lead was useful. 

One of the things I love about these pencils is the lead. I may have mentioned this before but I hate having to constantly sharpen pencils. With the Blackwing 602 pencil, I was able to sharpen it to a fine point and it would keep that fine point for a long time before starting to dull. 

It’s hard to give specifics of how long it lasted. But when it comes to pencils keeping a sharp point this was much better compared to Staedtler pencils and other coloured pencils that I have used. 

There was the other added advantage that I didn’t have to worry about the graphite in the pencil breaking. With some pencils, you have to take care to not drop them because the graphite will break while in the core of the pencil. The pressure from the sharpener can also cause some pencil leads to break. 

I’m happy to say that I didn’t have any issues like this with the Blackwing 602. It can get really frustrating if you’re trying to sharpen a pencil and the lead breaks constantly. 

### Cost Of The Palomino Blackwing

Probably one of the main downsides to the Palomino Blackwing pencils is the price. The Blackwing pencils seem to be slightly cheaper if you live in the US. At $28.29 for a box of 12. They are much harder to come by in the UK. On Amazon, they can be anywhere from £45-60 depending on the seller. 

If you do live in the UK and want to try the Blackwing pencils I would recommend you check out The Journal Shop or London Graphics. Both sell the 12 pencil set for around £30. 

I think part of the reason the pencils seem so expensive is that they can only be bought in sets of 12. When you break it down it works out at £2.50 per pencil. Now, this is still very expensive for a single pencil. 

But when you look at other artist tools they work out to be around the same price. You can expect to pay £1.90 for an individual Derwent Procolour pencil. The Supracolour pencils from Caran d’Ache also work out at around £1.90 per pencil. 

Now obviously this isn’t an exact comparison. Blackwing pencils are still very expensive. Especially when you compare them to other writing pencils. 

Another high end writing pencil is the Tombow Mono. This works out as a much more affordable alternative to the Blackwing if you live in the UK at £15 for a box of 12. Still not what you would call cheap but much better than £30. 

Even this is still very expensive when you compare it to something like a set of Staedtler pencils at £4. Or the Muji Mechanical pencil which costs £1.50 and another £2.50 for lead refills. 

As much as I love using the Blackwing pencil I’m still finding it hard to justify that extra cost. Especially when there are similar alternatives at a much more affordable price range. 

### My Thoughts On The Palomino Blackwing

I haven’t tried out every pencil in the Blackwing range, so I can’t say for certain if they are all good. But I do genuinely like using this pencil. Which is a big thing considering I do everything I can to avoid using regular pencils. I’m not even joking. The last time I bought a bog-standard pencil was when I started college over 5 years ago. 

As nice as it is. I’m still not sure the Blackwing 602 pencil is worth the price. I wouldn’t be at all surprised if it is priced so high because of brand recognition. And the fact this is a product which goes all the way back to the 30s. Yeah, its a nice pencil and it’s comfortable to hold. But £30 is a lot of money for a set of pencils. 

I think its really one of these cases where you have to consider how much you will use the pencil. If a set of 12 pencils are going to last you three years then yes paying a bit more money might be worthwhile. But if you go through a pencil in a month, maybe you

# Blackwing Starter Pack (Christmas Special)

#### Nathan Hogg

 26 Dec 2022 — 4 min read 

As the year comes to a close, it is important that we take some time to look back at all the good that happened in 2022. For me, that includes passing calculus 2, not catching the flu from my family, and most importantly, getting a set of Blackwing pencils for Christmas. For the longest time, I have been a diehard mechanical pencil user, shunning those that stoop to using trees to write. I decided to take the plunge into this wooden world, and I am not disappointed.

The first time I used a Blackwing 602 pencil was when I was 14. I found it on the floor the first day I worked in my school theater's tech booth. I was amazed by the then-unfamiliar eraser mechanism and the smooth writing experience. I should have known, given the phrase "HALF THE PRESSURE, TWICE THE SPEED" is embossed into the side. When I adopted this pencil, it was no more than seven inches long. Since then, it has shrunk measurably, though it is still comfortable to use. 

The OG Blackwing 602

For Christmas this year, I asked for a pack of 602s, the One Step Sharpener, Soft Eraser, and Point Guards. I figured, might as well jump right in. I guess I was reasonably good this year, as I got what I asked for. Even though it has been two days since I got these items, I think I have used all of them enough to give a reasonably informed opinion.

Blackwing 602

To begin, I'll discuss the Blackwing 602 pencils. As someone who's only prior experience with wooden pencils was cheap Ticonderoga's or the random pencils that seem to spawn wherever you need them, these are like writing with butter. The "Firm" graphite in the 602 is smooth, but not too smooth. It hits right in that sweet spot.

Samples of the 602's graphite As seen above, this pencil puts down a dark, smooth line, and shades very well. It also is reasonably smudge-resistant, which is a pleasing change of pace from my usual 2B daily drivers. The end of the pencil features Blackwing's signature paint brush style ferrule, and holds a pretty sizable eraser, and a clip that allows it to be extended as it wears down.

Blackwing One-Step Long Point SharpenerAs expected, wooden pencils require the use of a pencil sharpener, and Blackwing just so happens to offer several on their website. The one I have is the "One-Step Long Point Sharpener." It comes in a very nice matte black aluminum finish with a coarse knurling at the top to help grip when sharpening. They say that the canister can hold the shavings from sharpening 3 brand-new pencils. I did not test this, but I am inclined to believe them. 

A knolled view of the sharpener

This is hands down the best sharpener I have used, which isn't saying much, but its the thought that counts. They sell replacement blades, and given how sturdy this thing is I can see myself using it for years to come.

Blackwing Handheld Soft Eraser and Holder 

Next up is the Blackwing Handheld Soft Eraser and Holder. As the name suggests, this is a soft eraser. It performs very well when compared to what most are familiar with, the Pentel Hi-Polymer eraser. This offering from Blackwing has a major leap over the Pentel, with the convenient and handy holder. It is made of aluminum and features the same clip mechanism seen on the pencils that allows this eraser to stay in the holder until it is just a nub. This is a luxurious take on the traditional cardboard sleeves most block erasers come in.

Test of the Eraser on various lead grades 

Above are the results of my testing. One pass over a dark swatch from the 602, 0.7 B, 0.5 2B, and 0.3 H leads on Rhodia paper. The results were applaudable, as this was from only one pass. I was surprised to see that the eraser got did the best on the H swatch.

Blackwing Point GuardsFinally, we have possibly the most useful accessory, the Point Guard. These are cleverly designed so that the lead of your pencil "floats" inside, so that the long points don't chip or break all together. They do extend the length, so beware of that. They are made of a very nice machined aluminum, and come in matte black, silver, and gold.

Overall, I am beyond satisfied with these items. With that being said, I am seriously reconsidering my mechanical pencil loyalty, as hard as that is to say. 

I hope everyone has a safe and happy holiday season and new year!

# Blackwing 602 Pencil Review 2026: Still Worth It?

 By Zoe Ward October 29, 2026 October 29, 2026 

The Blackwing 602 has a reputation that arrives before the pencil does. People call it the writer’s pencil, the composer’s pencil, the pencil John Steinbeck kept in a jar on his desk. That kind of hype creates a problem. 

A pencil costs under three dollars, yet this one carries decades of legend on its gunmetal barrel. So the real question in 2026 is simple. Does the 602 write well enough to justify the price, or are you paying for a story? 

I bought a 12 count box, sharpened every pencil, filled three notebooks, and pushed it through daily writing, sketching, and margin notes. This review covers the feel, the flaws, the alternatives, and the exact situations where the 602 earns its spot.

Table of Contents

## In A Nutshell: 

- The graphite is firm, dark, and genuinely smooth. The 602 lays down a clean line with light pressure. The old slogan “Half the Pressure, Twice the Speed” actually describes the writing feel well, which is rare for marketing copy.
- Point retention is the strongest selling point. Compared to softer art pencils, the 602 holds a usable tip through roughly a page and a half of normal handwriting. You sharpen less and write more.
- The square ferrule and replaceable eraser are useful, not just decorative. You slide the eraser out, extend it, and keep going. Replacement erasers are sold separately in multiple colors.
- It is expensive for a wooden pencil. A 12 count box sits around 30 to 36 dollars depending on the seller, which works out to roughly three dollars per pencil. A Ticonderoga costs a fraction of that.
- The eraser is the weakest part. It smears more than a dedicated block eraser and it wears down fast. Serious erasing still needs a separate tool.
- Buy it if you write by hand daily. Skip it if you only need a pencil for test bubbles, shopping lists, or a drawer backup.

## Blackwing 602 Pencils, Firm Japanese Graphite, Gunmetal Gray, 12 Count

This is the core product in the lineup and the one most people mean when they say “Blackwing.” The barrel is finished in a pearlescent gunmetal gray with gold hot stamped lettering that reads Blackwing 602 along one flat. Inside sits firm Japanese graphite, milled for consistency and blended to resist crumbling. The casing uses sustainably sourced California Incense cedar, which sharpens cleanly and smells faintly sweet when you cut it. The square gold ferrule holds a pink replaceable eraser. Each box of 12 doubles as a pencil cup once you tear off the lid, which is a small touch that I ended up using on my desk. All Blackwing products conform to ASTM D 4236 safety standards.

## Unboxing The Blackwing 602

The box feels better than it needs to. It is a sturdy cardboard sleeve with the Blackwing logo printed in silver, and the lid lifts off to reveal twelve pencils resting in a paper tray. Nothing rattles. My set arrived with no chipped finish and no dings on any ferrule, which matters when you are paying premium prices.

The first thing you notice is the barrel shape. It is hexagonal but with wider, flatter facets than a standard school pencil, so it sits differently between your fingers. The second thing is the weight. The 602 feels slightly heavier than a Ticonderoga, likely from the denser core and the metal ferrule.

Pencils arrive unsharpened. Factor that in if you are gifting a set.

## Build Quality And Materials

The cedar is the headline material here. Incense cedar is softer than the basswood used in budget pencils, so the barrel peels away in long ribbons instead of splintering. Over twelve pencils I had zero core breaks during sharpening, which is the real test of whether a graphite core is properly centered and glued.

The lacquer finish is applied in several coats and feels slick rather than tacky. It did pick up small scuffs after a week rolling around in a bag, so it is not scratch proof. The gold stamping stayed crisp.

The ferrule deserves its own mention. It is a flat rectangular clamp rather than a round crimp, and it grips the eraser firmly with no wobble. It also stops the pencil rolling off a sloped desk, which is a genuinely practical accident of design.

## Top 3 Alternative for Blackwing 602 Pencil

## Writing Feel On Paper

This is where the 602 justifies most of its price. The core glides without the waxy drag you get from cheap graphite, and it does it without feeling slippery. On Rhodia dot paper the line comes out dark and even. On cheap copy paper it still performs, though the softer tooth means you will sharpen a little more often.

Light pressure produces a dark line. That single property changes how long you can write before your hand gets tired. I noticed it most during a two hour note taking session, where my grip stayed relaxed the whole time.

The graphite is firm by Blackwing standards, not by pencil standards overall. It sits somewhere around a B in traditional grading, darker than a standard HB but not soft enough to smear constantly.

## Point Retention And Sharpening

A firm core means a tip that survives. In my testing the 602 held a writing usable point through roughly 150 to 200 words of cursive before the line noticeably widened. That is strong for a pencil this dark.

Sharpening is where things get opinionated. A standard school sharpener works, but it wastes the pencil’s potential. The 602 is built around a long curved point, and a long point sharpener gives you more usable graphite per sharpening plus a finer tip for small handwriting.

One honest warning. Cheap plastic sharpeners with dull blades will chew the soft cedar and occasionally snap the tip. A sharp German steel blade solves this completely. Budget for a decent sharpener alongside your first box.

## The Square Ferrule And Replaceable Eraser

The clamp style eraser is the 602’s signature feature. You pinch the ferrule tabs, slide the eraser up as it wears, and eventually swap in a fresh one. Replacement packs come in several colors and cost a few dollars.

This system is better than a crimped eraser in one way and worse in another. Better, because you never reach that dead stub stage where metal scratches your paper. Worse, because the flat eraser has less surface area than a rounded one and erases in thin strips.

Performance is average. It lifts light marks well. It struggles with heavy, pressed in lines and tends to leave a gray ghost. I keep a separate block eraser on the desk for anything serious.

## Blackwing 602 vs Pearl, Matte And Natural

Blackwing sells four core graphite grades, and picking the wrong one is the most common buying mistake. The 602 is the firm core. It is the writer’s choice, best for handwriting, journaling, and note taking where point retention matters.

The Pearl sits in the middle. It is softer than the 602 but firmer than the Matte, and it suits people who want a darker line with reasonable longevity. The Pearl also runs slightly more matte and less shiny on the page.

The Matte is the softest and darkest. Artists, sketchers, and music composers gravitate to it because it shades beautifully, though it needs constant sharpening.

The Natural uses extra firm graphite in an unfinished cedar barrel. It is the closest thing to a precision pencil in the family.

## Who Should Buy The Blackwing 602

- HALF THE PRESSURE, TWICE THE SPEED - The motto of the original 602. Firm, smooth Japanese graphite holds its point longer and delivers crisp, smudge-resistant lines.
- THE PENCIL THAT MADE BLACKWING FAMOUS - John Steinbeck wrote with it daily, Chuck Jones animated Bugs Bunny with it, and composers scored with it. Try out the pencils coveted by award-winning creators.

Buy this pencil if you write by hand every day and actually notice the difference between tools. Journalers, novelists drafting longhand, students who take paper notes, and crossword solvers all get real value from the combination of a dark line and a lasting point.

It also makes an excellent gift, because the packaging and the history give it more presence than the price suggests. A box of twelve lands well with a writer or a stationery fan.

Skip it in a few situations. If you need pencils for a classroom set, for kids, or for scantron sheets, the cost makes no sense. If you sketch and shade heavily, the Matte core serves you better. If you only pick up a pencil twice a month, a cheaper option will feel identical to you.

## What The Blackwing 602 Does Not Do Well

An honest review needs this section. The price is the main problem. At roughly three dollars per pencil you are paying six to ten times what a quality mass market pencil costs, and the writing experience is not six times better. It is maybe thirty percent better, which is a real gap but a subjective one.

The eraser underperforms. It smears graphite rather than lifting it cleanly, and the thin profile wears down faster than expected.

The finish scratches. Toss a 602 loose in a bag and the lacquer picks up marks within days.

Smudging is also real. The dark core transfers onto the opposite page in a closed notebook, and left handed writers will drag their hand through fresh lines more than they would with a harder pencil.

## Pros And Cons

A quick side by side for easy scanning.

- Firm graphite writes dark with very light pressure, which reduces hand fatigue during long sessions.
- Point retention is excellent for a dark core, so you interrupt your work to sharpen less often.
- California Incense cedar sharpens cleanly with almost no core breakage or splintering.
- The square ferrule holds a sliding replaceable eraser and stops the pencil rolling off your desk.
- Build consistency across a 12 count box is high, with centered cores and an even finish.

- The price per pencil is high compared with mainstream alternatives that perform respectably.
- The eraser smears heavy marks and wears down quickly, so you still need a b

# Blackwing Pencils Review

I like pencils. I mean, I really like pencils. A 4B is my favourite, though I often sketch with a mechanical pencil with 2B lead because I’m quite lazy and like to forgo sharpening when possible. I’ve tried all sorts of pencils, often adding a couple of new ones when I make an art supplies order in an effort to find The One. And in my internet wanderings, I’ve heard many times about Blackwing pencils, but up to now have never taken the plunge.

Blackwings seem to have taken on a somewhat mythical status, with lots of illustrators claiming they’re the best pencil they’ve tried. I won’t go into their full history because it’s easy to find out for yourself with a quick Google, but basically it’s an old brand dating back to the 1930s that went out of production in the nineties, only to be revived by Palomino recently, hence them now being called Palamino Blackwings.

The sustainable cedar wood of these pencils comes from California, whilst the core is from Japan. They’re slightly longer than most pencils, at nearly 8″ (though they get shorter quickly, since they need sharpening often) and they have a pretty swanky, and effective, eraser, which can be replaced if necessary. It seems like you can get various special editions, but the three most available pencils are the original Blackwing, the 602, and the Pearl so these are the ones I tried.

Blackwings are most often available in boxes of 12, priced at aroundabout £20.00 – £25.00 which isn’t expensive on a per pencil basis, but is a bit of an investment if you’re not sure what you’re getting. The good news is, it is possible to buy them singly. I found them for £2.49 each from Foyles (and tried to resist buying a stack of picture books at the same time). They arrived well packaged in bubblewrap and sturdy cardboard, so well done Foyles (I’ve received pencils with broken lead in the past and it’s SO annoying).

The pencils arrived unsharpened, but they’re standard width, so any decent sharpener will do the job. First I did some quick scribbles to see how they felt, and what the difference was between the three models.

Blackwings don’t follow the usual grading of HB, 2B, 3B etc but these three do offer different levels of firmness. I could immediately tell that whilst they differed in hardness, they were all very smooth, and somewhat blacker than some pencils I’ve used. Next I did a little graded scribble with each pencil, starting light, and gradually pressing harder to achieve the darkest shade I could.

As you can see, the dark part of the 602 scribble is not as black and the other two, whilst the original and the peal have less variation between them.

Finally I did a little sketch with each pencil, just a quick cat, to see how each one behaved. The three tests combined told me that the firmest of the three is definitely the 602, which, though still softer than an HB, is probably the best one if you’re after a smooth, dark pencil to write with.

I’m not sure I have a favourite at this stage, I think I shall have to use them and over time work out which one, or two , meets my needs the best. Maybe there’s a place for all three on my desk. Frankly, they’re all lovely, and I’m very happy to welcome them into my art arsenal, or artsenal, if you will. I think the hype is justified, and I certainly would recommend trying them out if you too are a pencil fan. They’re not going to change your life, but they are a pleasure to use, and to look at, and I shall certainly be investing in a box or two when I’ve worn these guys down to little nubs. In addition to my mechanical pencil, of course.
